article.title: Why I don't buy 538's new election model
article.subtitle: It barely pays attention to the polls. And its results just don't make a lot of sense.

extraction.summary: Silver critiques G. Elliott Morris's new 2024 538 presidential model, arguing it puts most of its weight on fundamentals (apparently about 15:85 fundamentals-to-polls nationally) even though its own published error bars show the fundamentals are less reliable than the polls. He says its state forecasts, such as Wisconsin and Ohio, fall outside the range between the polls and the fundamentals, and that its uncertainty is far too wide. He lays out the Silver Bulletin approach for contrast. A polling 'snapshot' is regressed toward a fundamentals prior (economy plus incumbency), with roughly a 70/30 polls/fundamentals blend as of mid-July. The model also separates 'drift', meaning poll movement before Election Day, from 'error', meaning Election Day poll miss. Silver argues drift is smaller in the polarized era, that fundamentals should be a weak prior, and that 538's drift chart is inflated because it uses noisy state polls back to 1948.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model first builds a polling-based 'snapshot' of the current race, then regresses that snapshot toward a prior based on 'fundamentals'.
findings.evidence_quote: First, we take a current “snapshot” of the race — which is based on polling, although with some fancy adjustments to smooth out the data in states where there isn’t much polling — and then regress it toward a prior

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin snapshot includes adjustments that smooth out the data in states with little polling, combining state and national polls to give a more precise picture.
findings.evidence_quote: fancy polling averages that 538 or Silver Bulletin do, which can combine state and national polls to give you a much more precise snapshot of the race

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, the fundamentals prior consists of the economy and incumbency.
findings.evidence_quote: “fundamentals” (which in our case consist of the economy and incumbency)

findings.statement: As of July 18, 2024, the Silver Bulletin model blends the polling snapshot and the fundamentals roughly 70/30 in favor of polls. The national calculation is (-2.0 x 70%) + (2.5 x 30%) = -0.6, so Biden is projected to lose the popular vote by about 0.6 points.
findings.evidence_quote: Currently, our model uses roughly a 70/30 blend of the snapshot and the fundamentals.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin fundamentals model has Biden favored in the 2024 popular vote by roughly 2.5 points. The 538 fundamentals model has Biden ahead by 3.3.
findings.rationale: Silver believes the incumbency advantage has diminished in the polarized era.
findings.evidence_quote: My fundamentals model has Biden favored in the popular vote by roughly 2.5 points, whereas Morris’s has him ahead by 3.3.

findings.statement: In July 2024, Biden's Electoral College position in the Silver Bulletin model was considerably worse than his popular vote standing, implying a Republican-leaning Electoral College bias.
findings.evidence_quote: Biden’s Electoral College position is considerably worse than his standing in the popular vote

findings.statement: On July 18, 2024, the Silver Bulletin forecast gave Biden a 28 percent chance of winning, while 538 gave him 53 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: Biden’s chances are probably lower than the current 28 percent in the Silver Bulletin forecast

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin model implicitly assumes the candidates run a normal campaign and does not account for Biden possibly dropping out or being unable to campaign normally. Silver therefore thinks Biden's true chances are lower than the model's 28 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: he’s probably not capable of running the sort of normal campaign the model implicitly assumes he can

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin model separates two sources of uncertainty. 'Drift' is how much the polls will move between now and Election Day. 'Error' is how well Election Day polls capture the actual result.
findings.evidence_quote: First, there’s how much the polls will move between now and Election Day. This is what we call “drift” in our forecast. And second, there’s uncertainty in how well Election Day polls will capture the actual result — what we call “error”.

findings.statement: In the current highly polarized era, poll drift is much smaller than it once was, because few votes are up for grabs and polls settle on their final margin earlier. Election Day error can still be large, as in 2020 when polls underestimated Trump.
findings.rationale: Polarization reduces the number of persuadable voters.
findings.evidence_quote: in a time of extremely high polarization, “drift” is much less than it once was: the polls hone in toward their final margin earlier since few people’s votes are actually up for grabs

findings.statement: Silver implies that drift estimates should be calibrated toward recent, polarized-era elections rather than pooling polls back to 1948 equally, because polls are much less swingy now.
findings.evidence_quote: their estimates of polling movement are derived from polls since 1948 — but polls now are much less “swingy” than they once were

findings.statement: Morris often cites a 538 chart of expected absolute change in state polling-average margins (1948-2020) by days before the election. It shows about 9-10 points of expected change from 300 to about 150 days out and about 9 points at 155 days. The change declines slowly to about 8 points near 75 days, then falls rapidly to 0 on Election Day.

Silver says 538's drift chart badly exaggerates future poll movement because it is based on state polling averages. Those are noisy since each state is polled only a few times a month or less, so much of the measured movement is statistical noise rather than real change in the race.
findings.evidence_quote: Much of what a state polling average captures is just statistical noise, not real movement in the race.

findings.statement: Silver says the 538 2024 model gives polls very little influence before roughly Labor Day. Its forecast moved toward Biden after the June 2024 debate even though 538's own polling average moved about 2 points toward Trump.

quantities.name: 538 polling average shift toward Trump since debate

findings.evidence_quote: Biden has actually gained ground in their forecast over the past few weeks even though their polling average has moved toward Trump by 2 points!

findings.statement: Nationally, 538's full forecast was Biden +2.6. That falls between its Election Day polling forecast (Trump +1.9) and its fundamentals (Biden +3.3), which implies about a 15:85 polls-to-fundamentals weighting.
findings.evidence_quote: Whereas our mix is roughly 70:30 in favor of polls, theirs is apparently about 15:85 in favor of fundamentals.

findings.statement: In Wisconsin, 538 had a polling average of R+2.2, an adjusted and Election Day polling forecast of R+2.7, and fundamentals of D+0.2. Yet its full forecast was D+1.3, outside the range of both components. Ohio showed similar behavior. Silver calls this nonsensical and possibly a bug. 538 attributes it to 'patterns of overperformance in similar states'.
findings.rationale: A blend of two components should lie between them.
findings.evidence_quote: 538 projects Trump to lead the polling average by 2.7 points in Wisconsin on Election Day. And it thinks the fundamentals basically show a tie

findings.statement: When blending two or more components into an average, a model should place more weight on the more reliable component. 538's fundamentals error bar is wider than its polling error bar, yet it seemingly gives fundamentals 85 percent of the weight.
findings.evidence_quote: it’s almost axiomatic that if you’re blending two or more components into an average, you’ll want to place more weight on the more reliable component

findings.statement: The 95 percent interval on 538's national fundamentals-only forecast spans roughly Trump +20 to Biden +30. Silver calls these results nearly impossible in today's polarized environment.
findings.evidence_quote: covers everything from roughly Trump +20 to Biden +30 (!), results that are nearly impossible in today’s highly polarized political environment

findings.statement: In July 2024, 538 gave Biden a 14 percent chance of winning the national popular vote by double digits. The Silver Bulletin model gave 1.4 percent.

quantities.name: Silver Bulletin P(Biden wins popular vote by 10+)

findings.evidence_quote: they say that Biden has a 14 percent chance of winning the national popular vote by double digits. Our model says the chances of that are just 1.4 percent

findings.statement: 538's 95th percentile forecast range in Pennsylvania ran from roughly Biden +18 to Trump +17, which Silver says is almost certainly too wide. 538's Pennsylvania median was D+0.6.
findings.evidence_quote: 538’s 95th percentile forecast covers outcomes ranging from roughly Biden +18 to Trump +17

findings.statement: With very wide uncertainty, tipping-point probabilities default toward states with many electoral votes. 538 ranked Texas (40 EVs) as the 3rd-most-likely tipping-point state at 9.8 percent, ahead of Michigan (9.1 percent) and Wisconsin (6.6 percent).
findings.rationale: Electoral vote counts are known exactly, while the polling is uncertain.
findings.evidence_quote: we know exactly how many electoral votes Texas has (40) while the polling is more uncertain

findings.statement: Silver treats fundamentals as a weak prior that should be discarded fairly eagerly once enough polling exists. Strong priors are risky in data-poor settings such as presidential elections, which happen only once every four years.
findings.rationale: Fundamentals-only models have a poor out-of-sample track record.
findings.evidence_quote: Morris treats the fundamentals as a strong prior and I treat them as a weak one that you should be pretty eager to discard once you get enough polling

findings.statement: Election models based on fundamentals alone have a poor out-of-sample track record, doing not much better than a random guess.
findings.evidence_quote: Models based on fundamentals alone have a poor out-of-sample track record, not doing much better than a random guess.

findings.statement: Fundamentals models cannot account for potentially material candidate-specific factors such as Biden's age, because the sample is too small. Silver's hypothetical: with 1,000 elections you might find candidates over 80 underperform fundamentals by 3 points. Congressional data might help. Without such an estimate, this is a reason to trust polls more than fundamentals.
findings.evidence_quote: if you can’t, it’s at least a reason to trust the polls more than the fundamentals

findings.statement: A model should not be judged as having 'won' based on a single election outcome, since a sample of one cannot validate probabilistic forecasts.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsound model is validated because it “won” the model wars based on a sample size of one election

findings.statement: Design flaws and bugs in election models are often hard to detect through backtesting alone and usually surface only under real-world stress tests. Examples are sign flips, misentered polls (such as an Alabama poll coded as Arizona), and complicated components that combine to be less than the sum of their parts.
findings.evidence_quote: it’s often hard to detect these design flaws through backtesting alone — usually you only learn the hard way once a model is stress-tested under real world conditions

findings.statement: Silver says the 2024 538 model should not be read as a polling-based model. Its output mainly reflects the incumbency prior, so it says little about whether Biden's polling is fine.
findings.evidence_quote: you shouldn’t really think of the 538 model as a polling-based model at all

findings.statement: If neither polls nor fundamentals are considered reliable, Silver says it may be better not to publish a statistical forecast until later in the race, rather than publish one that effectively defaults to 50/50.
findings.evidence_quote: perhaps that a reason not to publish a statistical forecast of the election until later in the race

findings.statement: 538's published component chart may hide steps. It shows a forecast of the Nov. 5 polling average, not the actual result, so Election Day poll error may be added separately.
findings.evidence_quote: their chart only shows what they forecast the polling average to be on Nov. 5, not the actual result

findings.statement: The FiveThirtyEight model of 2008-2022 is now the Silver Bulletin model, since Silver retained the IP when he left Disney. The 2024 538 model is a new model built by G. Elliott Morris and has no real-world track record.
findings.evidence_quote: what was formerly the FiveThirtyEight model from 2008-2022 is now the Silver Bulletin model — I retained the IP when I left Disney

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling average accounts for each poll's quality, sample size and recency. Averages are adjusted based on trends in both state and national polls. On July 18, 2024, the national average was Trump 43.3, Biden 41.2 and RFK Jr. 8.0.

political_insights.insight: In the polarized era, presidential polls barely move. In 2012 and 2024, the polls stayed stable despite major events such as a felony conviction, a debate disaster and an assassination attempt.
political_insights.evidence: The Silver Bulletin 2024 national average stayed roughly flat from March through July 2024.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Use small drift variance relative to historical estimates from 1948 onward.

political_insights.insight: The presidential incumbency advantage has considerably diminished in the polarized era.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Reduce the weight on incumbency in the fundamentals prior.

political_insights.insight: In 2024, Biden's Electoral College position was considerably worse than his popular vote position.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model state-level structure rather than just the national vote.

political_insights.insight: Biden's age is a potentially highly material factor that fundamentals cannot capture.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Trust polls more when idiosyncratic candidate factors are present.

open_questions: How the Silver Bulletin 70/30 polls/fundamentals weight evolves over time until Election Day (its functional form).
The magnitude and time decay of the Silver Bulletin drift parameter versus its error parameter.
The specific economic indicators and incumbency treatment in the Silver Bulletin fundamentals model.
How the Silver Bulletin smooths sparse state polling (state-national trend adjustment details).
What mechanism ('overperformance in similar states') caused 538's state full forecasts to fall outside both components.
